samples.text:
The line graph shows how many cinema tickets were sold in one country from 2000 to 2024. The pie chart shows the main ways adults watched films in 2024.

Overall, the tickets sales were quite stable for many years but they fell a lot in 2020. In 2024 most adults watched films by streaming.

In 2000, 142 million tickets were sold. This number rise to 171 million in 2004 and then it stayed around 170 million until 2016, with 164 million in 2008, 172 million in 2012 and 168 million in 2016. However, in 2020 the sales dropped dramatically to only 44 million, which was the lowest point. After that, it recovered to 121 million in 2024 but it was still lower than in 2000.

The pie chart shows that streaming services was the most popular way to watch films, with 58% of adults. The second was broadcast TV with 18%, and cinema was only 12%. Download or rental had 9% and DVD or Blu-ray was the least popular with 3%.

To sum up, the cinema is not very popular way for watching films nowadays.
samples.why: Basic overview near the start · key features covered with accurate figures · adequate but simple linking · some repetition and imprecise wording · errors in verb form, agreement and articles, plus a weak ending.

samples.text:
The line graph shows the number of cinema tickets sold in a particular country between 2000 and 2024, and the pie chart illustrates the main ways in which adults watched films in 2024.

Overall, ticket sales were relatively stable for most of the period before collapsing in 2020 and only partly recovering. Meanwhile, streaming was by far the most common way for adults to watch films in 2024, with cinema attracting only a small minority.

In 2000, 142 million cinema tickets were sold, and this figure rose to 171 million in 2004. For the next twelve years, sales fluctuated only slightly, ranging between 164 million and 172 million. In 2020, however, they plunged to just 44 million, around a quarter of the 2016 level. By 2024 they had recovered to 121 million, although this remained below the figure for 2000.

Looking at the pie chart, 58% of adults mainly used streaming services to watch films, which is more than all other methods combined. Broadcast TV was the second most popular option, at 18%, while the cinema was the main choice for only 12% of adults. Downloads and rentals accounted for 9%, and just 3% of people still mainly watched film on DVD or Blu-ray.
samples.why: Clear overview linking both visuals · key features highlighted with useful comparisons (a quarter, more than all others combined) · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary · one minor slip.

samples.text:
The line graph traces annual cinema ticket sales in one country from 2000 to 2024, while the pie chart identifies the main way in which adults watched films in the final year.

Ticket sales held up well for most of the period but slumped dramatically in 2020 and had not fully recovered by 2024. By that year, streaming had become the dominant means of watching films, with the cinema a relatively marginal choice.

After rising from 142 million in 2000 to 171 million in 2004, sales plateaued, remaining within a narrow range of 164 to 172 million until 2016. This stability ended abruptly in 2020, when sales plummeted to 44 million, roughly a quarter of the 2016 figure. A partial recovery followed, lifting sales to 121 million in 2024, still some 21 million short of the 2000 total.

The pie chart shows that streaming services were the main source of films for 58% of adults, more than three times the share for broadcast TV (18%), the next most popular medium. Only 12% of adults chose the cinema as their principal way of viewing films, while downloads or rentals accounted for 9% and physical discs such as DVDs and Blu-rays for a mere 3%.
samples.why: Well-placed overview synthesising both visuals · key stages selected skilfully with accurate derived figures · cohesion managed smoothly · precise vocabulary (plateaued, marginal, medium) · wide range of structures, error-free.
